title: The Seal and the Stranger
subtitle: a story of itsdangerous, in six chapters
premise: A server must hand a value to a stranger (a browser, an email inbox) and later take it back. It cannot keep a copy. How does it know the stranger didn't change it?

chapters.title: Once upon a time, there was a message

characters: want_bytes, who turns everything into bytes
facts: Everything is turned into bytes before any work is done.
A Signer holds a list of secret keys, oldest to newest, even when given one key.
The salt defaults to b'itsdangerous.Signer', and salt=None also gives that default.
The separator defaults to b'.' and may not be a character of the URL-safe base64 alphabet.
The default algorithm is HMAC over SHA-1, and SHA-1 isn't looked up until it's used.
open_questions: Why may the separator not be a letter?
Why keep a list of keys if only one is used to sign?

chapters.title: The seal
inputs: chapter 1: the Signer, its keys, salt, separator and algorithm

facts: Signing uses the newest key only.
The key is derived: by default sha1(salt + b'signer' + secret_key).
A signed value is value + sep + base64(HMAC(derived_key, value)), with the '=' padding stripped.
The value itself is not hidden. Signing is not encryption.
answers: Why the separator may not be a letter: the signature is written in that alphabet.

chapters.title: The gatekeeper
inputs: chapter 2: the shape value.sig and how a signature is made

facts: unsign splits on the LAST separator, so the value may contain separators.
Every key is tried, newest first. Old keys can still verify; only the newest signs.
Comparison is constant-time.
A failed check raises BadSignature, which still carries the untrusted payload.
answers: Why a list of keys: rotation.

chapters.title: The scribe
inputs: chapters 2-3: sign and unsign, for bytes only

facts: dumps = serialize to bytes, then sign. loads = unsign, then deserialize.
The Serializer's default salt is b'itsdangerous', not the Signer's.
loads tries each signer from iter_unsigners and raises the last BadSignature if all fail.
Deserializing happens only after the signature is verified.
The timestamp is signed along with the value: value.ts.sig.
Timestamps are packed as big-endian ints with leading zero bytes removed, then base64'd.
An age above max_age, or below zero (signed in the future), raises SignatureExpired.
An expired signature stops the fallback loop; the next signer isn't tried.
The payload is compact JSON, zlib-compressed only if that saves more than one byte, then base64'd.
A leading '.' marks a compressed payload.
loads_unsafe returns the payload even when the signature is bad, which is why the library is called itsdangerous.
outputs.epilogue: The whole journey of one token, from dumps to loads.
